title: Tuba and bass on the Hines records, and the move to four-beat
summary: He used tuba for ballads; four-beat came in gradually.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Some of the photos, the old photos of the band, show you with the string bass, then there's tuba on the stand behind you.
All the records are, as far as I can tell, all the ones that I have, you play bass on all the records except "Madhouse," and, interestingly enough, "Blue Because of You." You play tuba on those two.
Well, I used to use the tuba a lot for ballads, sustained notes.
I don't know. Tuba just automatically went out. The band stopped using the tuba, and got right down to the string bass.
Wouldn't -- some of the earlier records, you know, you're playing two-beat. And some of the later ones there's more four-beat.
Yeah. And then some are mixed. Was that four-beat style -- come in just gradually, or did the guys say, look, let's play four, it swings more, or what?
I don't know how -- I can't remember how that four-beat style came in. Just automatically come in
I guess different bass players started it.

Yeah. Well, some of the early records, say the Louie Armstrong records with Earl and Zutty Singleton, Zutty's playing four -- four/four on the bass drum. Which gives it, you know, a nice lift to the whole thing. But I've always been curious about, you know, how that transition came in.
How that transition came in? I really can't recall how that happened. It could have been due to different drummers, you know, coming in with their style of drums.
